accounting.rationale: J3/24-007 PDF 77, printed 63, lines 3-6: introductory declaration terminology, permissions, attributes, and the Clause 8 cross-reference are separated below. This paragraph does not prescribe a new diagnostic.
PDF 77 line 3: a type's name serves as a type specifier. The actual specifier productions and restrictions are owned by 7.3.2.1 and their defining alternatives.
PDF 77 line 3: a type name may be used in declaring objects of that type, subject to the defining type and declaration rules. This is not permission to instantiate an abstract type.
PDF 77 lines 3-4: a declaration may specify the type of a named object; the syntax and other attributes are not supplied by this introductory sentence.
PDF 77 line 4: explicit declaration is an admitted route. Clause 8, including 8.2, defines that route; no duplicate S requirement or admission-only program is fabricated here.
PDF 77 line 4: implicit declaration is an admitted route, under the mapping and exclusions of 8.7. This does not override IMPLICIT NONE.
PDF 77 lines 4-5: type is not an object's only attribute. Rank, type parameters, and other properties are treated in 8.1/8.5; a type specifier alone is not a copy-all-attributes operation.
PDF 77 lines 5-6 directs the reader to Clause 8 for declaration mechanisms and specification of type and other attributes. Those rules retain their ownership.

PDF 77 lines 7-8 defines the homogeneous scalar-element model of an array, including common type and all type parameters. It is not a new array-constructor grammar or a promise that any mixture of types is admissible.
PDF 77 line 7: scalar data of intrinsic type can form an array. The named intrinsic types, supported kinds, and actual construction/association rules remain dependencies.
PDF 77 line 7: the element model also includes nonintrinsic types, not just derived types; enum and enumeration types must not be silently dropped.

PDF 77 lines 7-8: an array and its elements have the same type. This whole-array relationship does not erase the declared/dynamic-type distinction for polymorphic entities in 7.3.2.3 or the separate construction rules in 7.8.
PDF 77 lines 7-8: the same relationship includes all type parameters, not only KIND or only LEN. Parameter classification and establishment remain with 7.2, 7.4, 7.5, allocation, and association.

PDF 77 lines 9-10 defines variables and their value domain, with an assignment cross-reference. It supplies neither a concrete numerical oracle nor compulsory reporting of every invalid value or operation.
PDF 77 line 9: a variable is a data object. The distinction from named constants remains in the defining data-object rules.

PDF 77 lines 9-10: both type and type parameters determine the values available to a variable. The specific value sets and representation qualifications are owned by the relevant type definitions, not duplicated here.
PDF 77 line 10 identifies assignment (10.2) as one way to change a variable's value, not the only way and not a local definition of assignment conversion, allocation, or finalization.

PDF 77 line 11 relates a variable's type to the operations available on it. Intrinsic and program-defined operations and their interfaces remain governed by 7.4, 7.5.11, Clause 10, and Clause 15. A valid arithmetic example would not prove this whole relation, and no catch-all negative is justified by this paragraph.
